title: Card CTA
summary: Use a Card CTA to offer one next step, such as setting up UPI or rating an insight, with a title, a short line, and a button.

anatomy.title: A prompt, its button, and an icon
anatomy.description: The cta type splits a white panel in two: the title, the body, and a button take 3/5 of the width, and an icon sits in the rest. rating and sip keep the title, body, and button, and add their own parts, shown under Configuration.

configuration.title: Three types, and the button’s look
configuration.description: type sets the layout: cta, the default, puts the title, body, and button beside an icon; rating adds a badge above and like and dislike beside the button; sip adds an avatar and a line of facts above the button. Props for one type do nothing on the others. iconSlot, buttonSlot, ratingBadgeSlot, ratingActionsSlot, and avatarSlot replace a type’s parts and get the card’s modes. The button is always purple at size S: Emphasis makes it lighter, and Semantic Intent System gives it and the icon AppearanceSystem’s status colour. AppearanceBrand changes only the rating badge. Context CTACard enlarges the icon, and Page type SubPage and context 8 Section add a grey border.

states.title: Rating with or without Save
states.description: The card itself isn’t pressable; its buttons are. On rating, showButton={false} removes Save and moves like and dislike to the start, and showRatingActions={false} removes like and dislike. Like and dislike only respond when you pass onPressLike and onPressDislike. The card’s button can’t be disabled.
specimen: Paying your bills on time helped. Was this useful?

sizing.title: Your layout sets the width
sizing.description: The card fills its host’s width; Figma and Storybook draw it at 320 px. On cta the text takes 3/5 of the width and the icon 2/5, padded 22 px top and bottom. Height follows the text: nothing cuts the title or body short, so longer copy or a narrower host makes the card taller. The button grows with its label and never wraps.
blocks: More text, a taller card: nothing cuts it short.

content.title: The offer, what it gives, and a verb
content.description: Make the title the offer, the body what the person gets, and the button label a verb, such as Set up, Save, or Start SIP. Keep the title to one line and the body to three: the card doesn’t cut either short. On sip, the headline names the plan, the description is its main fact, and the subtitle qualifies it.

sources.title: Use the public Card CTA contract
sources.description: The guide compares the Figma component with the installed package and its Storybook stories.
blocks: Installed jfs-components is 0.1.78 (16 October build) from the team’s private package repository. Figma’s Card/CTA has the same three types, but its CTA type shows a badge, a caption line, and a full-bleed picture, while the package’s cta shows an icon and no badge or caption; a picture passed through iconSlot isn’t clipped to the card’s corners. Figma’s rating badge is purple because that variant sets AppearanceBrand Secondary; the package’s is gold until you pass it. Nothing cuts the title or body short, a long button label runs out of the card, ratingMediaAlign doesn’t move the default badge, and without avatarSource sip shows a stock photo. On the web the default button adds a hidden 9,999 px copy of its label that makes a page scroll sideways unless something around the card clips it, so these examples sit in hosts that clip (all reported). The published Storybook still shows the older generated page.
